title: The Shunammite (2 Kings 4:8–37)
hook: a woman builds the prophet a room and asks nothing: "I dwell among mine own people"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elisha asked for pi shnayim, and picked up an old cloak lying on the ground. Did you carry on a piece of someone's good work? Today, Elisha is on the road, and a woman in the town of Shunem notices him. Day seven hundred seventy-two.
screen: `AN OLD CLOAK LYING ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: A bed, a table, a stool and a lamp. That's the whole list, and the text gives it item by item. A woman in Shunem, described as a great woman, has been inviting the traveling prophet Elisha to eat whenever he passes through. Then she goes further. She says to her husband: this is a holy man of God who keeps passing by. Let's build him a small room on the roof, with a bed, a table, a stool and a lamp, so whenever he comes, he has a place to rest. No one asked her to. She saw a traveler who kept passing by, and made room.
screen: `A MEAL WHENEVER HE PASSES.` → `A SMALL ROOM ON THE ROOF.` → `A BED, A TABLE, A STOOL, A LAMP.`

segments.voice: One day Elisha is resting in that room, and he wants to repay her. He sends his servant Gehazi with an offer. You've taken all this trouble for us. What can be done for you? Shall we speak for you to the king, or to the captain of the army? It's a real offer. A word from a prophet in the right ear could open doors. And her answer is quiet and complete: "I dwell among mine own people." Thank you, but I'm fine. I live among my own people. She isn't looking for a connection at court. Her hospitality wasn't an investment. Elisha doesn't let it go, though. Gehazi points out that she has no son, and her husband is old. So Elisha calls her and tells her: about this season next year, you will hold a son. Her reply is startling: no, my lord, do not lie to your handmaid. She had never asked for it. And the son is born. The story doesn't stop there. When the child has grown, he goes out to his father in the field and cries, my head, my head. He is carried to his mother, and dies on her lap. She carries him up to the little room, lays him on the prophet's bed, shuts the door, and rides straight to find Elisha. Asked on the way whether all is well, she says only: it is well. Then at Elisha's feet the grief pours out. Elisha comes, prays, stretches himself over the child, and the boy sneezes and opens his eyes. And look where the miracle happens: in the room she built for a stranger. The space she made out of kindness, asking nothing, became the place where her son was given back to her.
screen: `WHAT CAN BE DONE FOR THEE?` · then, large: `I DWELL AMONG MINE OWN PEOPLE.` · then: `DO NOT LIE TO THY HANDMAID.` · `THE PROPHET'S ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make space for a guest. Look around the room you're in. Think of the spaces you have: a spare chair, a corner of a table, an hour on a weekend, a seat beside you at lunch. Then think of someone who passes through your life a little tired: a new coworker, a neighbor living alone, a relative who visits, a friend who's been quiet. What would the Shunammite's small room look like for them? It doesn't need to be big. A plate, a chair, a time to sit. Plan how you'd set it out, expecting nothing back. The bell holds the time.
The Shunammite. The woman of Shunem who built a small room for a traveling prophet and, offered a favor at court, said she dwelt among her own people. Today's word.
Your line: I dwell among my people. Today, make a little room for someone, a chair, a plate, a few minutes, and don't keep score. Day seven hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Jews read the story of the Shunammite as a haftarah alongside the Torah reading of Abraham's welcome to his guests, and welcoming guests, hachnasat orchim, is honored as a mitzvah.

original.note: Hebrew: among my people I dwell, her answer in 2 Kings 4:13.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a miracle child.
what it means: a woman makes room for a stranger, asks nothing, and the room becomes the place of her son's life.
what a scholar hears: her husband asks why go to the prophet on a day that is neither new moon nor sabbath (4:23).
